433.t: DownBeat's target audience and free student subscriptions
433.s: Alkyer describes readers by psychographics, with musicians first and then fans, and the free copies and digital subscriptions given to students.
433.q: Yeah. People always ask me for demographics, and I go I can’t give you demographics. I can but DownBeat is a psychographic. We use psychographics. People who are educated or will be educated, love music, generally play music or have played music or will play music, want the better things in life,…

805.t: Students at live concerts and Kind of Blue
805.s: Woods describes students converting to jazz at live shows; Cobb says young people come to jazz through 'Kind of Blue', and Woods calls 1959 a high-water mark.
805.q: It’s one of the most exposed albums too, in the world, through the years. So that adds to the validity of what we were saying about exposure.

561.t: Jazz, black culture, and the Marsalis revival
561.s: Gitler says radio and television co-opted jazz from the black community, and credits Wynton Marsalis and Art Blakey's group with a renaissance rooted in tradition.
561.q: Well I think it has surfaced in jazz because I’ve written about this also and no one has really picked up on it. I thought that the continuity of jazz in the black community was kind of co-opted by radio and television. I don’t say that rhythm & blues wasn’t great, I used to enjoy it very much, and…

928.t: Reaching young audiences and the shortage of places to play
928.s: Playing for schoolchildren, few swing musicians left and no small joints for young players to learn.
928.q: Gee, I wish I could answer that one. But you’re doing what you can by having these archives and trying to expose the kids to letting them hear some of the stuff live. I’ve been playing a few elementary schools and high schools and little kids love it. It’s amazing how little kids, first graders,…

656.t: Jazz in schools and young audiences
656.s: Schools have exposed generations to jazz, and Brubeck concerts sell out with young listeners.
656.q: Well that’s the reason why I think it’s growing — it’s actually growing. It’s getting bigger all the time. Because the schools have had this music in it since I was in grammar school. So its effect is taking hold and that is a whole series of two generations, maybe three generations of kids have…

1003.t: Would he write an 'Is Jazz Dead?' article
1003.s: He is reluctant to take on the perennial question, calling jazz an evolving Black-American art form and pointing to thriving schools.

447.t: Hopes for jazz's future and the lost club training ground
447.s: Optimism about jazz, and how club sink-or-swim experience trained him.
447.q: You know I have to be somewhat optimistic and say that I think it will, because it’s lasted a lot longer than a lot of people thought it was going to last now, and just hopefully it will appeal to a younger generation — at least maintain the status quo that it has now.

740.t: The future of jazz and loss of outlets for young players
740.s: He is optimistic but wants more outlets, noting earlier players learned in dances, circuses and movies.
740.ch: Influences and the future of jazz
740.q: I think it’s doing wonderful. In fact I think it’s making tremendous progress in more ways than one. You don’t have all the — everything changes, the setting. A lot of the settings have changed you see, especially since the beginnings of jazz. But things are supposed to change. But even in the…

961.t: San Diego's current jazz scene and its Latin influence
961.s: Wofford calls the local scene perilous, with major clubs lost but fine players and university programs; Latin music has grown only recently.
961.ch: San Diego and the state of jazz
961.q: Well I think it’s like most cities its size across the country. The jazz scene is perilous at best and from one year to the next it’ll be better than others. Right now it’s not great. We’ve lost a couple of what were the major clubs here. There is always activity and there are wonderful players…

472.t: Future of jazz and education for kids
472.s: Heath is confident jazz will survive, citing Monk Institute competitions and kids' programs.
472.q: I think jazz will be here forever, I don’t see it going anywhere. There’s too many people, young people, that are playing the music and being connected with the Thelonious Monk Institute, as I am on the board of trustees for many years; I see musicians every year. I was very fortunate to be, not…

219.t: Where the future jazz audience will come from
219.s: Wein expects it to come from the pop generation and older fans, not from schools.
219.q: I think the future of jazz does not lay with that. The future of jazz, the audience is gonna come out of the rock generation when they get tired of hearing the same shit all the time and start looking for something else. So you'll have, you will have a minority. Jazz has always been a minority…

614.t: Audience reception of the new album on campuses
614.s: The album is getting a great reception, especially in colleges where students asked about it for months before.
614.ch: Instruments, tenors and the current band
614.q: Yeah, we've had great reception. Now it's just starting to get into the hinterlands where we usually spend our time. And finding out some of the more youthful reservoirs, like I suppose in colleges, that they are now asking, and when you play it you get a tremendous reception. And maybe they…

412.t: The golden age and the lack of small clubs
412.s: Hodes says he came in during a golden age of entertainment. Young players today lack small clubs to learn in.
412.q: But when I came in, it was still the golden age of, not only jazz, but entertainment. We had Clayton Jackson Durrant. How many people caught an act in person? I did. And -- I mean, who are around. And I've become an antique. Look, he's still breathing. But I can --
